newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-Afghan leader dies in oblivion in Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Afghan leader dies in oblivion in Moscow.

text.p: Former Afghan communist leader Babrak Karmal, who personified the Kremlin's ill-fated nine-year intervention in Afghanistan, has died of liver cancer in oblivion in Moscow.
Moscow-based Afghan journalist Iskander Khatmani, who had close links with Karmal, told Reuters that the 67-year-old former leader, died on Tuesday in Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital.

Ekho Moskvy radio station said Karmal's body would be flown on Friday to Mazar-i-Sharif for burial. The Afghan town is the capital of a vast area controlled by ethnic Uzbek warlord Rashid Dostum who helped Karmal in the past.

The Kremlin installed Karmal in power in December 1979, after its troops invaded Afghanistan and Soviet commandos killed the then leader Hafizullah Amin during the storming of his residence in the capital Kabul.

Karmal, the son of a regional governor, had been a leftist revolutionary in his university years. He tried hard but with little success to turn his mountainous Moslem country, ruled by age-old tradition, into a tightly-controlled Soviet-style communist society.

But he overdid his subservience to Moscow and the war against Islamic guerrillas backed by the West and Iran raged on. He was replaced by former secret police chief Najibullah in November 1986, a time when Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev was keen to broaden public support for the pro-Moscow government.

Yuli Vorontsov, Moscow's ambassador to Afghanistan in the late 1980s, said in later television interviews that the country was run to a large extent by Soviet "advisers" who even wrote minor public speeches for Karmal and Najibullah.
Soon after his removal from power, Karmal left for Moscow for what was described at the time as "medical treatment" and he had spent most of time in Moscow since then.
Moscow officials made little secret of the fact that his departure was exile and an attempt to protect its loyal servant from his many foes in Afghanistan.

About 200 members of the Afghan community in Moscow, most of whom served in Karmal's government, attended a memorial service on Thursday in the city's Central Clinical Hospital -- where Russian President Boris Yeltsin was also treated.
Gorbachev, who played a key role in Karmal's dismissal and ordered the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Afghanistan in 1989, was the only prominent Russian figure to mark his death.
"This man tried very hard to reflect the interests of the Soviet Union in Afghanistan, but as a politician he proved to be out of place," Ekho Moskvy quoted Gorbachev as saying.
"He (Karmal) started pushing this country in a Marxist direction and imposed on it a model which could not be accepted," he said.
Gorbachev said he did not believe that Karmal's death would in any way influence the political situation in Afghanistan, where rival groups are fighting for control of Kabul.

The hardline Islamic group Taleban seized Kabul on September 27, executing Najibullah and his brother. Forces loyal to Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani and Dostum are trying now to win the city back.
